needs: An equation with a term that stops mattering: one part of a sum shrinks to nothing as n grows.

brief.title: The term that stops mattering
brief.idea: In a cost like n squared plus one hundred n, the smaller term dominates for tiny inputs but becomes a rounding error as n grows, which is why we write just n squared.

beats.say: Suppose a program takes n squared plus one hundred n steps to handle an input of size n.
beats.show: The expression n² + 100n appears, with its two terms in separate boxes.

beats.say: Which part matters more? It depends on n, so try a few sizes and compare the two parts.
beats.show: A table appears with columns for n, n², 100n and the share of the total that 100n makes.

beats.say: At n equals ten, n squared is one hundred, but one hundred n is a thousand: ninety one percent of the total.
beats.show: The first row fills in: 10, 100, 1,000 and 91%; the 100n box grows larger than the n² box.

beats.say: At n equals one hundred, both parts are ten thousand, so they split the cost evenly between them.
beats.show: The second row fills in: 100, 10,000, 10,000 and 50%; the two boxes are the same size.

beats.say: At a thousand, n squared is a million and one hundred n is a hundred thousand: nine percent.
beats.show: The third row fills in: 1,000, 1,000,000, 100,000 and 9%; the 100n box shrinks.

beats.say: At a hundred thousand it is a tenth of one percent. The second term has all but vanished.
beats.show: The fourth row fills in with 0.1%, and the 100n box shrinks to a sliver beside n².

beats.say: Each time n grows ten times, n squared grows a hundred times, but one hundred n grows only ten.
beats.show: Arrows between the rows mark n² growing by 100 times and 100n by 10 times.

beats.say: So for large inputs we keep only the term that grows fastest, and write the cost as n squared.
beats.show: The + 100n part of the expression is crossed out, leaving n² alone.

beats.say: The smaller term was never wrong. It just stops mattering once n is big enough.
beats.show: The four shares are shown again in a column, shrinking: 91%, 50%, 9%, 0.1%.

beats.say: The same reasoning drops a constant too: twice n squared grows at the same rate as n squared.
beats.show: A second expression, 2n², appears and is written as O(n²) as well.
